label: Tensor Notation
notes: This short appendix, printed pages 562 through 564, fixes the index conventions that make the rest of the book compact. We meet covariant and contravariant indices, the summation convention, the epsilon tensor, and the multifocal tensors written in coordinate form so later incidence relations read as simple contractions.

label: Two Kinds of Index
notes: Distinguish upper and lower slots from the start. A point carries an upper, contravariant index because its coordinates scale inversely with the basis, while a line or plane carries a lower, covariant index because its components scale with the basis. That bookkeeping keeps proportionalities consistent through any change of frame.

label: Transformation Under a Basis Change
notes: Apply a change of basis given by a matrix and watch the two index types move oppositely. Contravariant coordinates transform by the inverse, covariant components by the transpose. The notebook solves and multiplies both, then confirms that a single scalar contraction returns the same number in either basis.

label: Einstein Summation Convention
notes: The convention is purely a labour saver: a symbol that appears once up and once down in a term is implicitly summed over its range, so we drop the summation sign. A repeated index is dummy and can be renamed; a free index survives and names the resulting object.

label: Contraction as the Core Operation
notes: Contraction is the engine of the whole notation. Summing a shared upper-lower pair glues two tensors and lowers the total order by two. Every incidence test in the book, a point on a line, a correspondence on the fundamental matrix, is just a contraction whose value should vanish.

label: Raising and Lowering Indices
notes: A metric or any chosen rank-three object lets us trade an upper index for a lower one and back. In projective vision there is no privileged metric, so raising and lowering is mostly done by the epsilon tensor, which converts between a vector and the antisymmetric object that represents the same geometric act.

label: The Levi-Civita Epsilon Tensor
notes: Epsilon is totally antisymmetric: plus one on even permutations, minus one on odd, zero when an index repeats. Contracting it with two vectors reproduces their cross product, and contracting it with three reproduces a determinant. The notebook checks both equalities to machine precision against NumPy.

label: Join of Two Points into a Line
notes: The flagship example: the line through two image points is their cross product, written with epsilon as l_i equals epsilon_ijk x^j y^k. The summed pair of upper indices produces a single lower index, exactly the covariant slot a line should carry. Duality gives the meet of two lines the same way.

label: The Fundamental Matrix in Index Form
notes: With indices the epipolar constraint is one contraction. Writing F with two lower indices, the relation x-prime to the i F_ij x to the j equals zero says corresponding points contract F to zero. The notebook ties this to the same antisymmetric machinery that built lines from points.

label: Trifocal and Quadrifocal Tensors
notes: Three and four views need genuine higher-order tensors. The trifocal tensor carries one lower and two upper indices, T_i jk, and contracting it with a point and two lines transfers and constrains entities across three images. The quadrifocal tensor extends the same pattern with four indices to four views.

label: Notation as Working Code
notes: The payoff is that index strings become einsum strings. Free indices name the output axis, repeated indices are summed, and the appendix verifies every claim numerically: scalar invariance, epsilon cross products, and slice contractions all match explicit loops. Carry this habit into every multi-view derivation that follows.
